comment: Every identity permitted to author or commit in this repository.
This is an allowlist, deliberately, and not a list of banned addresses. The
incident that produced it involved one corporate address the owner knew about;
auditing the history for it turned up a second corporate domain from a former
employer that nobody had thought to look for. A denylist only ever blocks the
leak someone already noticed. An allowlist blocks the one nobody has.
Both `author` and `committer` are checked. They differ on rebases, amends, and
web merges, so validating one leaves the other free to carry anything.
Every commit, back to the root. There is no exemption.
This field previously named a cutoff commit, because twenty-one commits
across two non-approved corporate domains sat in history that was already on
`main`. The owner chose to rewrite instead, while the repository was private:
`dev`, `main` and all nine other branches were rewritten in place, mapping
both domains onto the owner's declared identity. Trees were unchanged, so no
file moved; only authorship metadata did.
That is why this is `ROOT` and not a SHA. The old cutoff pointed at a commit
the rewrite made unreachable — it still resolved on the machine that did the
rewrite, where the object lingered, and would have failed on any fresh clone.
A stale cutoff is worse than none: it fails closed in CI while passing
locally, which is the hardest kind of disagreement to diagnose.
`ROOT` is a positive claim, not the absence of one. If any commit anywhere in
history stops matching this list, the check fails.

identities.note: Primary identity. The default for all work in this repository.

Forge-provided no-reply address for the same account. Authors commits created through the GitHub web interface.
Committer on merges performed through the GitHub web interface. Never an author.
